Classroom action research · 2026 · Unpublished manuscript
Reconsidering assessment evidence
After an AP Biology assessment, my students corrected their explanations using feedback. I could see
what they changed, but I could not tell which causal relationships they would be able to explain
without that support. I introduced structured reflection and, later, an independe

Unit 2
Unit 2 assessment and reflection
The Unit 2 question asked students to explain a proposed pathway from chytrid-related disruption
of sodium transport across amphibian skin to dehydration. After feedback, they revised their
answers and reflected on one difficulty, a transferable idea, and a preparation plan.

Preparation before Unit 3
Students reported what they actually did to prepare. These were self-reports, so they gave me an
account of preparation without documenting every study activity independently.

Reflection specificity and later explanations
For the 21 students whose Unit 2 explanations did not meet the completeness criteria, I examined what they
wrote about their earlier difficulty during feedback-assisted reflection. Twelve identified a particular
difficulty in their reasoning; the other nine offered different kinds of reflections. The table shows how each
group was classified on the subsequent Unit 3 assessment, which concerned a different biological
mechanism.

Seven of the ten later reconstructions met the item's completeness criteria. The four rows describe how they
differed from their originals, a distinction that would be lost if only the later classifications were considered.
Feedback and the more explicit prompt prevent these differences from establishing why students' explanations
changed.

How my practitioner judgment developed
I examined four practitioner reflection records alongside the student work. Notes A and B were written
during the classroom inquiry. The first distinguished students’ reports of preparation from the explanations
they could produce without feedback. The second documented my decision to retain original Unit 3
responses for later comparison, together with a concern that the more explicit reconstruction prompt might
change what students wrote.

page_previews.first:
Notes C and D were written during retrospective analysis after grades were finalized. Comparing the
response pairs showed that later completeness classifications concealed different earlier relationships and
contradictions. I could identify more specific questions for subsequent assessment, although I could not
determine how much of the difference came from correction, the changed prompt, or other
page_previews.last:
y expressed, while others no longer repeated
earlier contradictions.
Evaluating the adjustment therefore involved two judgments. The paired records helped me decide which
causal relationships and competing accounts required further assessment. They did not establish why
students’ responses differed, or whether the adjustment improved their understanding. This distinction
became the central lesson of the action research, changing how I interpreted the evidence generated by my
own intervention and what a subsequent inquiry would need to examine.
